Atsugewi Band (Pit River Tribe)

Also find this entry through: Atsugewi Band

The Atsugewi Band is one of the Pit River Tribe’s eleven autonomous bands. This starting guide connects the Tribe’s definition of band authority with the documented public work of Elder Lillian Snooks. It offers one historical community example while leaving fuller band-authored history and contemporary perspectives open for further research.

Read the sources [1] Pit River Tribe [2] National Park Service

Names & relationshipsThe Pit River Tribe names Atsugewi as one of eleven autonomous constituent bands. This individual band route is distinct from broader language/people labels and from the collective tribal government. No claim that each band is a separately federally recognized government or that the collective four-county statement defines this band’s boundaries.
A source guide for a deeper dive.This entry provides a brief orientation and an organized reading path. A comprehensive deep dive has not yet been completed. Follow the annotated sources and distinguish primary community accounts from outside reference material.

Source & image record ↗ · NPS-credited official photograph; public-domain reuse under the qualified NPS ownership policy

The exact NPS biography identifies Snooks as an Elder of the Atsugewi band and captions this public craft demonstration as 1996, with credit NPS/Dave Ashcroft and no separate third-party copyright notice for the photograph. The NPS ownership policy says material created by NPS is generally public domain unless otherwise indicated, while expressly excluding some third-party material. This is not a blanket claim about all NPS content or a CC0 designation. Root and an independent reviewer inspected the specific credit, policy and complete offered 650 × 971 frame. This is the supplied provider image; a larger original was not inspected. No pixel edit, crop, resize, recompression, retouching or generation was performed. The same delivered frame serves the card and opened page; CSS may crop or overlay it, while the banner retains the full composition and source edge. This is one historical elder’s public teaching example, not all band members, current officeholding or a modern membership determination. Image review adds no substantive bibliography work.

  2. Lilian Snooks

These are selected starting points. The full annotated collection, source perspectives, inspection limits and remaining research questions follow below. A starting guide is not an exhaustive history or community endorsement.

01

An autonomous band within the Pit River Tribe

The Tribe’s posted constitutional text names the Atsugewi Band among its eleven component bands and describes band responsibilities for cultural matters and representation. This modern political route remains distinct from the broader Atsugewi language/people entry and the historical Atsuge regional label. Neither a linguistic classification nor one elder’s biography determines present membership or boundaries.

Read the sources [1] Pit River Tribe

02

A documented elder and public cultural teaching

Emma Chapman’s NPS biography identifies Lillian Snooks as an Elder of the Atsugewi band of the Pit River Nation. It describes her later cultural teaching and consultation with relatives after boarding-school policies disrupted language transmission in her childhood. The accompanying NPS photograph is captioned as a 1996 demonstration. This is a dated individual history, not a portrait of today’s whole band or evidence of current officeholding.

Read the sources [2] National Park Service

What needs further research

  • Seek additional band-authored histories and appropriately public contemporary perspectives beyond one historical elder example.
  • The 1996 photograph and 2022 biography do not establish current band roles, roster, fluency, population, boundaries or outcomes.
  • Historical Atsuge/Apwaruge and broader Atsugewi categories remain distinct from modern membership.
  • Community editorial review and fuller historical coverage remain unrecorded.

Constitution of the Pit River Tribe ↗

Publication: 1964 adoption; published text updated July 2005

Read the preamble and Articles I–II, VI and VII, including band powers. The Tribe publishes this text as adopted in 1964 and updated July 2005. It distinguishes the eleven-band political entity from language labels and recognizes band cultural authority. No complete 2026 legal consolidation, title survey or independent jurisdictional ruling is inferred.

Inspection: Content reviewed for the stated scope

Scope: Read the preamble and Articles I–II, VI and VII, including band powers. The Tribe publishes this text as adopted in 1964 and updated July 2005. Publication: Page updated2022-03-15

Chapman traces Lillian Bernice Snooks from Sherman Institute to family-led cultural teaching and consultation. This institutional biography is attributed; it is not a current language census or direct inspection of its underlying books and recordings.
